record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present, including appendices; it is a preprint.
record.tranche_reason: The paper experimentally refines multimodal scaling laws: it varies pairing at fixed per-modality data budgets, compares law forms on held-out fits, and argues that existing forms need pairing-aware qualification in its supervised multimodal settings.
record.gate_note: This tests scaling behavior in supervised multimodal classification and fine-tuning, not language-model pretraining across parameter, token, and compute scales. The paper also cites results from other studies; those cited findings are not recorded as rows. Fit metrics used to compare candidate laws are included only where they report how well the tested loss curves are predicted.
record.test_reason: In supervised multimodal classification and fine-tuning, the study shows that loss depends on the pairing fraction, which standard laws omit. It finds synergistic loss is gated rather than falling as an immediate power law. It shows that the choice of law form changes held-out prediction error. These results bear on V5 (the power-law form in another regime) and V7 (curves bend away from a single law and depend on setup). There is no language-model pretraining and no extrapolation across orders of magnitude.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Also: the authors conclude that synergy acquisition is gated, requiring a paired-data threshold before synergistic loss falls, unlike immediate power-law decay. They state that pairing is an independent variable affecting loss. The '3.2% vs 10.4%' figure is the overall p=1 test.
record.recipe_differences: The original sources study language-model scaling; this paper studies supervised multimodal classification and fine-tuning at fixed architectures and parameter counts, varying data pairing and fitting candidate multimodal laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss curves depend on pairing fraction, test-time modality presence, data budget, paired-data presentation order, number of paired exposures, and in some results architecture. Candidate-law fit also varies with synergy gating, effective counts, shared exponents, and PID-pinned weights.

fits_no_version.finding: Unpaired data reduces redundant and modality-unique loss but never synergistic loss. Its value rises with the number of available pairs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multimodal data scaling, only paired data reduces synergistic loss; paired and unpaired data are initially complements.

fits_no_version.finding: In Digits, encoder architecture shifts the paired-example threshold at which S-digit accuracy leaves chance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Synergy-acquisition thresholds depend on encoder architecture.

record.code_released: https://github.com/airsplay/lxmert (published model code is cited; release of this paper's experiment code is not stated)
record.problems: The experiments are supervised multimodal tasks, not language-model pretraining. The authors state that larger data and parameter scales and self-supervised generative pretraining were not investigated. Several curve results are presented in figures without exact values in the text; fit comparisons are limited to the reported experimental grids.
record.rows_left_out: No additional reported outcomes bearing directly on the tested versions were left out. Figure-only curve values are described qualitatively where the text gives the trend; individual unreported values were not estimated from plots.

untested.parts: All of it: there is no language-model pretraining sweep over N, D or C.
All of it: held-out tests extrapolate only about 2x in data within the grid, not orders of magnitude.
All of it: there is no compute-optimal N/D allocation. The pairing-fraction optima under price budgets are a different quantity.
All of it: architecture and width variants are not matched at fixed parameter count.
Image/video generative pretraining, self-supervised regimes, repeated-data scaling, and parameter scaling. Only data scaling at a fixed N in supervised multimodal tasks is tested.
Parameter counting, training schedule and tokenization choices. Only data pairing and law-form choices are tested.

missing.what: Unimodal power-law data fits L(D)=EN+B·D^-β with exponents (Digits β 0.684/0.732; VQA 0.095/0.411). These bear on V5, but no fit-quality figure is given.
Interpolation tests (Leave-One-Out and Full fit). Four-channel variants reach 0.8–2.1% overall error versus 2.0–3.6% for published extensions, which is further evidence of law-form dependence.
Per-environment D↑ errors showing the four-channel advantage is not uniform (Digits: Shukor 9.6% vs four-channel 8.6–10.6%).

record.verdict_notes: This is supervised multimodal classification at fixed N, with data ranges spanning about 1–2 orders of magnitude. The authors explicitly exclude self-supervised pretraining and larger scales. The V2 links were removed because the held-out test extrapolates only about 2x. The reader's V2 labels are dropped.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model pretraining sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute with the other resources non-bottlenecked.
The paper tests prediction on held-out, higher-data runs within its experimental grids, not prediction across orders of magnitude or to much larger language-model pretraining runs.
It studies pairing fractions under data or price budgets, not loss-minimising parameter and token allocations as a function of compute.
It varies architectures and head widths, but does not establish comparisons at a fixed parameter count over a wide range of architecture details.
Tests supervised multimodal classification and fine-tuning; it does not test image/video generative pretraining, repeated data, language-model pretraining, or transfer generally.
No downstream-task performance relationship with pretraining loss or scale is tested.

The paper tests pairing effects and candidate-law fit dependence in its three supervised multimodal environments; it does not test language-model setup choices such as tokenization or large-scale pretraining schedules.

rows.subject: Digits
rows.size_stated: 483k trainable parameters (Appendix B.1); Table 1 reports CNN + 4-way head (476k).
rows.operation_detail: Swept pairing fraction at fixed per-modality data budgets and fixed compute; measured test cross-entropy.

conditions.value: k = 20 in Figure 2; k = 40 in the high-D channel analysis

rows.baseline: At p = 0, no paired examples; chance loss ln 10 ≈ 2.303.
rows.value: The text reports that increased pairing decreases loss; at high D the curve plateaus and then descends again as synergy is learned.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 2 shows ±1 std shaded bands; multiple seeds per combination (three for Digits).
rows.note: The result is a pairing sweep in a synthetic multimodal classification task, not a language-model pretraining scale sweep.
rows.check: This is a pairing sweep at fixed D and N, not a scale sweep, so it cannot show power-law form (V5). It bears on V7: data composition that existing laws ignore changes loss, and at high D the curve plateaus then descends a second time.

rows.subject: VQA-v2
rows.stage_stated: trained fusion head on frozen CLIP features
rows.operation_detail: Swept pairing fraction at fixed per-modality data budgets and fixed compute; measured test cross-entropy.
rows.baseline: At p = 0, no paired examples; chance loss ln 3129 ≈ 8.048.
rows.value: The text describes a large loss drop from p = 0% to p = 5%, followed by a more modest reduction as p approaches 1.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 2 shows ±1 std shaded bands; five seeds per combination.
rows.note: The authors attribute the initial drop to paired examples unlocking use of unpaired data; VQA is described as having a small synergistic share.
rows.check: This is a pairing sweep, not a scale sweep, so drop V5. Loss drops sharply from p=0 to 5%, then gradually. The interior optimum at k>20 is attributed to overfitting.

rows.subject: NLVR2
rows.operation_detail: Swept pairing fraction at fixed per-modality data budgets and fixed compute; measured test cross-entropy.
rows.value: The text reports that increased pairing decreases loss, with a flat-at-chance onset before loss falls; some seeds never leave chance, more often at lower p and lower D.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 2 shows ±1 std shaded bands; five seeds per combination, with failed-to-start seeds filtered from that figure.
rows.note: The onset and failed-to-start behavior make the result conditional on pairing amount and seed.
rows.check: This is a pairing sweep, not a scale sweep, so drop V5. The curve stays flat at chance before falling. Failed-to-start seeds were filtered from Figure 2, which is a selection choice.

rows.subject: Digits
rows.operation_detail: Tested individual information-channel losses with both modalities present and with irrelevant modalities nulled.

conditions.value: U1 image-unique, U2 audio-unique, R redundant, S synergistic
both shown versus irrelevant modalities nulled

rows.baseline: Figure 3 compares both modalities shown with the corresponding nulled-modality readouts; no single numeric baseline is stated.
rows.value: With modality presence matching, increasing pairing has no impact on U1 or U2 and slightly increases R loss; the authors state that paired data helps reduce synergistic loss. At low pairing, showing both modalities raises U1, U2, and R loss relative to showing one; readouts converge after around 8k pairs.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 3 reports plots; uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The direction depends on test-time modality presence; the paper distinguishes this from the synergy effect.
rows.check: This is a presence-matching control on channel losses versus pairing. It does not measure loss scaling with resources and does not compare law forms.

rows.subject: Digits
rows.operation_detail: Held paired data fixed and added unpaired examples; measured losses by information channel.
rows.baseline: At D = 8k, base loss is 1.26 nats; at D = 32k, the text says the same added-data ratio has little effect but gives no exact loss.
rows.value: At D = 8k, adding 24k images or audio clips reduces loss from 1.26 to 1.10 nats. Unpaired data reduces redundant and modality-unique loss but not synergistic loss; its effect is small at D = 32k.
rows.uncertainty: Uncertainty not stated for these comparisons.
rows.note: The paper reports the numeric total-loss change for D = 8k and qualitative channel outcomes.
rows.check: This shows which data stream reduces which channel's loss (1.26 to 1.10 nats at D=8k). It is not a power-law or law-fit test. Belongs in fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Digits
rows.operation_detail: Measured onset of synergistic-loss reduction as paired examples and paired exposures increased.
rows.baseline: Chance-level synergistic loss before the onset; exact numeric chance value not stated here.
rows.value: The authors estimate nfloor ≈ 2900 and r ≈ 40k for the interleaved mixture, and propose n* = max(nfloor, r/k). They report that the onset threshold decreases as the S-channel share of total loss increases.
rows.uncertainty: The estimates are approximate; no error interval stated.
rows.note: This is a gated departure from immediate loss decay, specifically for the synergistic channel.
rows.check: Digits synergistic loss stays at chance until about 2900 pairs or 40k paired exposures, then falls. This departs from immediate power-law decay, so V5 holds only after the gate and V7's bending is observed.

rows.subject: NLVR2
rows.operation_detail: Modeled the distribution of paired-example counts at which seeds leave chance accuracy.

conditions.value: paired-example count n* at chance escape
failed-to-start and chance-escape seeds in NLVR2

rows.baseline: Chance accuracy; no numeric baseline stated in this result.
rows.value: The reported model is log2 n* ∼ N (11.32, 1.362), with median n* = 2552 and χ2 fit p = 0.81.
rows.uncertainty: The distribution model includes 1.362 as reported; χ2 fit p = 0.81.
rows.note: The text characterizes NLVR2 gating as a random variable rather than a hard threshold.
rows.check: The NLVR2 chance-escape onset is a random variable (median n*=2552). The loss curve is gated rather than a power law from the start.

rows.subject: Digits, VQA-v2, and NLVR2 experiments (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: supervised multimodal classification; NLVR2 uses fine-tuning
rows.operation_detail: Fit candidate multimodal scaling laws and evaluated held-out fit tests.

conditions.value: four-channel law versus pairing extensions of published laws
fit tests, including held-out data-scale and pairing tests

rows.baseline: Pairing extensions of published laws: 10.4% error, as stated in the abstract.
rows.value: The proposed law: 3.2% error, as stated in the abstract.
rows.note: The paper's abstract reports these aggregate fit-test errors; this is not an orders-of-magnitude language-model extrapolation.
rows.check: Check the condition. In Table 3, 3.2% and 10.4% are the overall p=1 test errors: the best four-channel variant versus the best published extension (Aghajanyan +Cp). They are not errors across all fit tests. V5: a sum of per-channel power laws with a gate predicts well. V7: the choice of law form changes error roughly threefold.

rows.subject: Digits, VQA-v2, and NLVR2 experiments (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: supervised multimodal classification; NLVR2 uses fine-tuning
rows.operation_detail: Fit on lower data sizes and tested on higher data sizes; compared four-channel variants with published-law extensions.

conditions.value: Fit on D ∈ [0, Dmax/2) and test on D ∈ [Dmax/2, Dmax]

rows.value: The authors report that every variant of the four-channel law beats the published laws on D↑.
rows.note: This tests extrapolation within the experimental data range, not across orders of magnitude.
rows.check: The D↑ test extrapolates only from D<Dmax/2 to at most Dmax, a factor of about 2. It cannot show V2's orders-of-magnitude prediction, so drop V2. The 'every variant beats published laws on D↑' claim holds only in the Overall column (4.0–4.8% vs 5.1–9.0%). In Digits, Shukor's 9.6% beats several four-channel variants (9.8–10.6%).

rows.subject: Digits, VQA-v2, and NLVR2 experiments (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: supervised multimodal classification; NLVR2 uses fine-tuning
rows.operation_detail: Compared four-channel law variants and pairing extensions of published laws across held-out tests.

conditions.value: synergy gate, effective counts, shared exponents, PID-pinned weights

rows.baseline: Published-law extensions; no single baseline value stated for this comparison.
rows.value: The four-channel variants beat published laws on D↑ in all cases, on p = 1 in 14 of 16 cases, and on R2 in 13 of 16 cases. The authors report that synergy gating and effective counts help most; shared exponents also improve overall fit, while PID loss weights do not improve test performance.
rows.note: Results indicate that both the law form and fit choices affect predictive performance.
rows.check: Synergy gating and effective counts change held-out fit (Table 3); PID-pinned weights do not improve it. This is fit-choice dependence. The V5 link is weak because the row compares law forms rather than testing power-law form.

rows.subject: Digits CNN, MLP, and transformer variants
rows.size_stated: not stated for the MLP and transformer; main Digits model size is reported elsewhere
rows.operation_detail: Compared pairing-dependent loss curves and synergy onset across encoder architectures.
rows.measure: Synergistic-channel loss and S-digit accuracy versus paired examples
rows.baseline: Chance S-digit accuracy; numeric chance value not stated.
rows.value: The text reports consistent qualitative curve behavior, but S-digit accuracy first leaves chance at 16k pairs for MLP, 24k for transformer, and 32k for CNN.
rows.uncertainty: Uncertainty not stated in the text for these thresholds.
rows.note: Architecture changes the reported threshold; the experiment does not establish fixed-parameter comparisons.
rows.check: Architecture shifts the synergy threshold (16k, 24k, 32k pairs). Parameter counts are not matched, so this is not a V4 test.

relationships.reason: Loss sits at chance until a paired-data gate (about 2900 pairs in Digits; median 2552 in NLVR2), then falls. This is not an immediate power-law decay (r6, r7).
relationships.display_finding: Loss remained at chance until approximately 2900 pairs in Digits and a median of 2552 pairs in NLVR2, then began decreasing.

relationships.condition: Supervised multimodal tasks when loss is modelled as a sum of per-channel power laws in data
relationships.reason: The four-channel power-law sum predicts held-out p=1 loss with 3.2% overall error (r8). Fit quality is the only evidence; no direct log-log linearity is shown.
relationships.display_finding: The four-channel power-law sum predicted held-out p=1 loss with 3.2% overall error, although direct log-log linearity was unreported.

relationships.condition: Digits, VQA-v2 and NLVR2 at fixed N
relationships.reason: Pairing changes loss at fixed per-modality data (r1–r3). Curves are gated or plateau rather than following a single power law (r1, r6, r7). Held-out error depends on law form and fit options: 3.2% vs 10.4%, and gate and effective-count switches (r8–r10).
relationships.display_finding: Pairing changed loss at fixed per-modality data, producing gated or plateauing curves; law form and fitting options changed held-out errors between 3.2% and 10.4%, including sensitivity to gating and effective-data specification.
